doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Monsters of the Id and its updated lyrics
summary: The family recites the song, discuss its Forbidden Planet source and Costello's version.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Like, “Monsters Of The It” that he wrote in the ‘60s, when he sings that now...
“Monsters of the Id.”
You haven’t heard “Monsters Of The Id”? That’s one of my favorites. And when he sings that now, it’s all...
Costello did that.
He did it with me.
Amy did it with Elvis Costello on one of her CDs.
On one of her albums, Elvis Costello is singing “Monsters Of The Id.”
And people love that now, and they think he just wrote it for the political scene. I mean, it’s really... Well, you know all the lines to it.

Oh, do you want to hear the lines? “Monsters of id / No longer stayin’ hid / And terrors of the night / Are out in broad daylight / No need to lock the door...” No, wait a second. There’s a lot of words. Dad... “No need to...”
Wood.
Yeah, “...knock on wood / Don’t stop to say a prayer / They won’t do any good / They’re multiplyin’ in the air.” Then you have, like, “creatures from the deep / Are going without sleep.’
yeah.
“And phantoms of the dark / Have their own place to park.”
yeah.
“No need to cause a fuss / Don’t go and make a scene / They know what’s best for us / They’re fightin’ fire with gasoline.” Then there’s a really good one at the end. Let me see...
“Toothless majorette...”
No, I’m talking about the newest one.
[LAUGHS]
That’s #36, huh?
Mmm-hmm.

Oh, “The creatures From the swamp / Rewrite their own Mein Kampf / Neanderthals amuck / Just trying to make a buck / Goblins and their hags are out there waving flags / When will be rid / Of monsters of the id.”
When did you write that?
What a timely piece. Either year.
Either year.
Well, it sounds like the late ‘60s.
It also sounds like the Bush years.
Except no one would have been talking about the Id during the Bush years. Psychoanalysis was more au courant in the ‘60s.
Well, that’s right. In fact, sometimes I wonder if people know what the Id is.
Didn’t you get that from Forbidden Planet? Didn’t you say that the movie Forbidden Planet kind of inspired “The Monsters Of The Id” concept?
What?
The movie, Forbidden Planet, “Monsters of the Id.”
Oh, yeah. I got it from there, “Monsters Of The Id.” “Monsters Of the Id” was a hoot.
It turns out to be in Man rather than an external monster. Right? The monster is inside.

Let’s do another lyric. What’s another lyric you can think of, not one of the early ones... That’s a very involved song, a much more involved song than you were writing in the late 1950s, for example.
Yes.
By this time, it’s the kind of thing Bob Dylan might write—except I think I like yours a little better.

Well, I think even stuff where people would... Like, in the early ‘60s... I’m just picking any, like “Stop this world...” Certain opening lines that I think probably at the time were... Like,, “Stop this world / Let me off / There’s too many pigs in the same trough / Too many buzzards sittin’ on a fence...”
“Monsters Of The Id,” that’s it. It’s whole...
What’s interesting are the revisions you’ve made to the ending. “The goblins and their trolls are out there wavin’ flags...”
“Out to rig the polls.” Right?
Yes, or “trying to rig the polls.” “Vampire in a...”
“In a Volks”?
Volks.
“In a Volks, a toothless...”
Majorette?
“...majorette on the internet.” So you brought that up to date.
He does that with a lot of songs.
Yeah.
If you’re ok with it, I think it’s a singular opportunity to go over some of these lyrics with you.
